newsitem.title: GERMANY: German deputies urge end to blood-line nationality.
newsitem.headline: German deputies urge end to blood-line nationality.

text.p: A group of German parliament backbenchers urged Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition on Wednesday to give the children of foreign residents citizenship to help them integrate properly into German society.

Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and junior coalition partner, the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), agreed after the last general election to change current legislation to give immigrants' children the right to German nationality.
But since then, they have been bitterly divided over how to do this.

The backbenchers' proposal for dual nationality to foreigners born in Germany raised the prospect that German nationality would not only be inherited along blood-lines but could be acquired by birth in the country.
Peter Altmaier und Norbert Roettgen from the CDU called for swift legislation to allow foreigners' children to acquire German citizenship at birth.
At maturity they would have to choose between German citizenship and that of their parents' country, they said.
The group, who said they had support within their own party and among associations, church groups and other lobby groups, urged the coalition to make a decision by the end of June.

"People are afraid of immigration, but we're not planning to open the gates to an influx of immigrants," Altmaier told a news conference, calling for an end to "delaying tactics" that had led to prolonged debate on the issue but no action.

"We want to give foreigners a clear signal and we want a solution so that the children of foreigners can grow up as Germans," Roettgen said, conceding that the group may end up having to make a compromise on their proposals.

The backbenchers are faced with stiff opposition from the CDU's Bavarian sister party, the arch-conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), which wants to preserve the principle that nationality is inherited through blood lines.
Germany is the only major Western industrial nation to maintain the blood-line principle which is enshrined in an Imperial law dating back to 1913.
Interior Minister Manfred Kanther, who is also in Kohl's CDU, argues that children born in Germany should have a right to German citizenship but not dual nationality.

CDU general secretary Peter Hintze suggested amending the group's proposal to grant foreigners' children citizenship once they start school rather than automatically at birth so that the blood-line principle is not destroyed.

CDU/CSU deputy parliamentary leader Rupert Scholz proposed that children should be granted citizenship only if their parents apply for this and if they do, the children should be obliged to give up their parents' nationality.
